title: Six ways to be dear
hookLine: kindness in deed, word and thought, sharing, virtue and view held together

cards: Every group that lasts, a family, a team, a congregation, a group chat that's somehow survived ten years, has unspoken reasons it holds together, and every group that falls apart has reasons too.

The early monastic community knew both; monks quarreled, and the texts don't hide it. At Kosambi, one sutta says, the monks were stabbing each other with words, and the Buddha taught them this same list.
In the Book of Sixes he names six qualities worth remembering, because they create love and respect and lead to harmony, to unity, to not quarreling.
The Pali name is saraniya: things to be remembered, or things that make you dear.

teach.b: The first three are kindness, in three directions.
One: acts of body done with loving-kindness toward your companions, both in public and in private. Two: words spoken with loving-kindness, in public and in private.
Three: thoughts held with loving-kindness, in public and in private. That little phrase is the heart of it. Anyone can be kind when watched; what builds trust is the kindness nobody sees.
Whatever you receive, even the contents of your alms bowl, you share with those who keep the same practice, without holding back. For a monk who eats only what he's given, that's his meal.
Five: virtue held in common, the same precepts kept unbroken, the kind the wise praise. Six: view held in common, the understanding that leads out of suffering.
The order starts with what everyone can do immediately, a kind act, a kind word, and moves toward what grows slowly, a shared way of seeing. And none of the six is about getting others to like you.

They're all things you give. Being dear, in this sutta, isn't something you chase. It's what grows around someone who acts, speaks and thinks with kindness, shares, and keeps faith with a common path.

how: Buddhist monastic communities often teach the six saraniya dhammas as the basis of harmony in the sangha, and lay Buddhist groups sometimes take them as guidelines for family and community life.

games.q: six ways to be dear: tap the pairs.
p: things to remember, that make dear

s: the six ways are about getting people to like you
all six are things you give: kindness, sharing, keeping faith with a common path.
the sutta stresses kindness both in public and in private
the phrase repeats for deed, word and thought.
the early texts admit that monks quarreled
at Kosambi the Buddha taught these same six to monks who were quarreling.

games.q: you're a monk, and today's alms are in your bowl. a companion who keeps the same practice has nothing. what does the sutta describe?
o: keep it; you need your strength.
games.why: the fourth way to be dear is sharing whatever you receive, even the contents of your bowl, freely with your companions.

practice: Bring to mind a group you belong to, a family, a workplace, a team, a circle of friends, and picture the faces.
Think of one thing you could share with them, some food, some time, a skill, good news, credit for a job well done, and picture offering it freely, without keeping score.
Then, for a breath or two, wish them all well, quietly, in private.

wordCard.voice: saraniya. The Pali word for qualities to be remembered or cordial, the six things in the Book of Sixes that create love and harmony: kindness in body, speech and mind, sharing, virtue and view in common. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali saraniya: to be remembered, cordial; the saraniya dhamma are qualities that make people dear to each other.

carryVoice: Your line: one unseen kindness. The kindness nobody sees still counts. Day six hundred seventy-five, done.
